walkthroughs.body_html:
Some nuclei are unstable.

They have too many protons, too many neutrons, or just too much energy. To get more stable, they fire out radiation — this is called radioactive decay.

Decay is random: you can't predict which nucleus goes next, only the average rate.

Alpha (α): a helium nucleus. Heavy and +2 charged. Most ionising, but stopped by a sheet of paper or a few cm of air.

Beta (β): a fast electron from the nucleus, charge −1. Medium ionising, stopped by a few mm of aluminium.

Gamma (γ): a high-energy photon. No charge, no mass. Weakly ionising but very penetrating — needs thick lead or concrete.

The half-life is the time for half the radioactive nuclei in a sample to decay. After 1 half-life: ½ left. After 2: ¼. After 3: 1/8.

Background radiation is the low-level radiation around us all the time. Sources include radon gas from rocks, cosmic rays, food, and medical scans.
